one_liner: Small Linux C line reader over a raw fd; about 30-40% less user CPU than fgets or getline on large inputs.
what_it_does: Reads delimiter-terminated lines (any delimiter byte, e.g. '\n' or '\0') from an already open file descriptor using one fixed-size buffer chosen at rs_open(fd, bufsz, delim). rs_getline() returns a RAWSCAN_RESULT holding begin/end pointers into that buffer plus a type (full line, line without trailing delimiter, start/within/end of a line too long for the buffer, paused, eof, error). It is not a drop-in for fgets/getline: there is no FILE*, no copy into a caller buffer, no nul termination, and returned pointers can be invalidated by the next call unless the pause/resume feature is enabled.
how_it_is_fast: It bypasses stdio's double buffering by calling read(2) straight into its own buffer and returns pointers into it, copying only when a partial line must be shifted down (memmove). Delimiter search uses glibc's vectorized rawmemchr, made safe by placing a copy of the delimiter in a read-only sentinel page just past the buffer and writing a delimiter after each read's end, so the scan never needs a length check. The hot path is a small inline function that returns the pre-computed next delimiter position and peeks the following one; rawscan_static.h compiles everything into the caller's unit (10% faster than the shared library on 8-byte lines, no difference at 512+ bytes per the README).
when_to_use: Linux/glibc command-line filters that scan very large files line by line and do little work per line (prefix match, field split), where per-line reader overhead dominates.
Inputs with untrusted or unbounded line lengths: the buffer never grows, so a giant line is returned in chunks instead of exhausting memory as getline's realloc can.
Records with embedded nul bytes or a non-newline delimiter (e.g. find -print0 output), which fgets handles badly.
Code that can work on (begin, end) byte spans without nul-terminated copies.
when_not_to_use: Anything multi-threaded on one stream: the README says a RAWSCAN stream must be used by a single thread.
Non-Linux or non-glibc targets: it needs rawmemchr, sbrk/brk and mprotect; the CMake port to BSD, macOS, Windows, clang and MSVC is untested by the author.
Long-lived programs that open many streams: rs_open grows the data segment with brk(2) and rs_close is an empty function, so each stream's buffer plus two pages is never freed.
Programs where the line reader is not the bottleneck, or where Rust's bstr is an option: the author reports bstr is as fast or faster and only matched it with hand-written inline compare code.
Projects needing maintenance or a track record: version 0.1.4, 6 stars, last commit 2024-09-25, no issues filed.

integration.form: shared lib (librawscan.so via CMake) or header-only (include rawscan_static.h)
integration.min_toolchain: C11 (anonymous union in rawscan.h), CMake 3.13; developed with GCC; library built with -O3 -march=native
integration.platforms: Linux x86-64 tested; other systems not tested
integration.thread_safety: Not thread-safe per stream (README); rs_open also calls brk, which is not safe while other threads use malloc

gotchas: rs_open allocates with sbrk/brk behind malloc's back and asserts the current break is page-aligned; man brk(2) advises against mixing these calls with malloc, and the asserts vanish under NDEBUG (CMake Release adds it).
Returned line pointers are invalidated by the next rs_getline when the buffer is shifted or refilled; use rs_enable_pause / rs_resume_from_pause if you need them to live longer.
Line end points at the delimiter byte (inclusive), and lines are not nul-terminated; a final line without a delimiter comes back as rt_full_line_without_eol.
The read count is stored in an int, so buffers above 2 GiB are not safe.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: None of the catalogued filesystems-and-io siblings is a line reader: liburing and SPDK speed up the I/O submission path, and diskus, gdu and fclones are whole tools. Pick rawscan when the cost is splitting already-cached data into lines in a single-threaded C filter; combine it with a faster I/O layer only if reads, not scanning, dominate.
verified_claims_summary: First-party README: on a Ryzen 1700 with an 11.27 GB, 55.6M-line file already in the page cache, user CPU (mean of 10 runs, nice -n-10) was 1.60 s for rawscan versus 2.61 s for glibc fgets, 2.36 s for getline and 4.38 s for grep, matching the prefix '6fffbf42'. Only user CPU is reported, not wall time; the committed harness (source/tests) compares rawscan with a hand-inlined 3-byte compare and min1stchunklen=3 against fgets/getline using strncmp, and builds getline_test without the -march=native flag the others get, so the gap includes harness differences.
status_note: Stale since 2024-09-25 and a self-described learning project at v0.1.4, but about 1,000 lines of C under Apache-2.0, MIT or GPL-2.0 at the user's choice, so it is easy to vendor and fix.
